title: Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges
summary: Nine major shipping associations are lobbying the IMO for a single global carbon pricing mechanism, claiming regional regulations create "double charges." This industry-led push prioritizes financial predictability and minimizing compliance costs over accelerating genuine decarbonization efforts. Operators must still be held accountable for excessive carbon intensity and continued high-volume HFO usage, irrespective of a unified regulatory landscape.
content:
Nine of the world’s leading shipping associations have joined forces to push governments towards a global emissions deal, warning that a patchwork of regional regulations risks leaving shipowners paying multiple times for the same carbon emissions.

The joint intervention comes ahead of a crucial round of talks at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) later this month, with governments still divided over how to regulate and price shipping’s greenhouse gas emissions.

BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), Intercargo, Intertanko, the World Shipping Council, Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), Interferry, the International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) and the International Parcel Tankers Association (IPTA) have called for a single global framework that applies equally to vessels regardless of flag, ownership or trade.

“Shipping is a global industry requiring global rules applied equally to all ships,” the organisations said.

The groups warned that national and regional schemes could result in duplicated compliance requirements and multiple charges for the same emissions, undermining efforts to establish a level playing field.

They want an IMO agreement that rewards verifiable emissions reductions while giving shipowners sufficient flexibility to manage the transition to cleaner fuels, many of which remain commercially unavailable for much of the existing fleet.

The joint statement also calls for regulations that are fuel- and technology-neutral, enforceable and backed by clear incentives for investment in alternative fuels and energy-saving technologies.

The intervention comes after the IMO failed to secure agreement on its proposed Net-Zero Framework in October 2025, forcing governments to postpone adoption for a year.

The framework, which combines a global marine fuel standard with an emissions-pricing mechanism, remains the subject of negotiations over its cost, design and implementation.

The industry’s latest appeal follows growing concern over the spread of regional carbon schemes. Several African governments are moving towards their own shipping emissions charges, while European operators already face the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime regulations.

The nine associations warned that the lack of regulatory certainty is complicating investment decisions for shipowners, ports, fuel producers and financiers, particularly given the limited availability and high cost of lower-emissions fuels.

Governments will resume negotiations at the IMO’s greenhouse gas working group from November 23 to 27, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session from November 30 to December 3.

A further extraordinary session to consider adoption of the emissions framework could take place on December 4, subject to confirmation during MEPC 85.
